cards.front: Why can't scientists predict when one particular unstable nucleus will decay?
cards.back: Each decay happens at a **random** time, so one nucleus's decay time cannot be predicted. A large group still changes in a predictable way over time.
cards.hint: Compare one nucleus with a large group of nuclei.

cards.front: What is the **half-life** of a radioactive sample?
cards.back: The **half-life** is the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei in a sample to halve.

cards.front: Which type of radiation ionises most strongly?
cards.back: **Alpha** radiation ionises most strongly but travels only a short distance through air, and paper or skin can stop it.
cards.hint: Compare the three types in the ionisation and penetration table.

cards.back: An **alpha particle** contains two protons and two neutrons, so alpha emission lowers the proton number by two.

cards.front: What happens to a neutron during beta-minus decay?
cards.back: The neutron changes into a **proton** and the nucleus emits an electron. The proton number rises by one while the total of protons and neutrons stays the same.
cards.hint: Think about what changes in the nucleus and what is emitted.

cards.front: Why does gamma emission not change the element?
cards.back: Gamma is **electromagnetic radiation** released as a nucleus loses energy. It does not change the numbers of protons or neutrons, so the element stays the same.
cards.hint: Compare with what alpha and beta emission do to the nucleus.

cards.front: What is wrong with saying that random decay means a large sample has no predictable pattern?
cards.back: **Randomness** applies to individual nuclei. A large sample still shows a predictable pattern, such as its half-life.

cards.front: Which amount should you halve at each stage when finding how much radioactive material remains?
cards.back: Halve the **amount still undecayed**, not the amount that has already decayed.
cards.hint: Think about what the sample still contains at each stage.

cards.front: Which radiation penetrates furthest through material?
cards.back: **Gamma** penetrates further than alpha or beta and ionises least strongly. Thick lead or concrete reduces it but does not necessarily stop all of it.
**Ionisation** is when radiation removes an electron from an atom.

cards.front: How do you work out the number of half-lives that have passed?
cards.back: $\frac{\text{elapsed time}}{\text{half-life}}$. Use the same time unit for both values.

cards.front: A sample of $80\,\text{mg}$ has a half-life of $5\,\text{days}$. How much remains undecayed after $15\,\text{days}$?
cards.hint: Start by working out how many half-lives fit into the elapsed time.

cards.front: How does the activity of a radioactive sample change over one half-life?
cards.back: The **activity** halves in each half-life. Activity counts decays per second and is measured in becquerels ($\text{Bq}$).
A **thin sheet of aluminium** stops most beta radiation, because beta ionises less strongly than alpha and passes further through air.
